The nickel nanostrandsTM have a diameter range of 50 to 1000 nanometers.
The exterior nanocomposite configuration provided 25% better EMI shielding than the baseline control specimen.
The exterior nanocomposite specimens were 11% better at ESD protection compared to the control specimen.
The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and Young's modulus (E) of the nanocomposites did not change after exposure to the simulated 5-year space environment.
Failure of the nanocomposites occurred through 90° ply failure first, causing delamination in the 0/90 plies, leading to transverse matrix cracking and delamination in the ±45 plies.
The nanostrand layers were not damaged in any of the nanocomposite configurations tested.
Adding 5% volume fraction of nickel nanostrandsTM to a polymer resin can increase the specific conductivity of the composite by over an order of magnitude.
A thin film (0.1016 mm) containing 20% volume fraction of nickel nanostrandsTM in polyimide is capable of shielding about 80 decibels between 8 to 12 GHz frequencies.

The thin film containing 20% volume fraction of nickel nanostrandsTM in polyimide maintained 75 decibels of EMI shielding with a DC conductivity of 1,100 S/cm after exposure to a simulated space environment.
Spacecraft deployed for military purposes must be engineered to survive the harshest space environments, including radiation, charged particles, and electromagnetic phenomena.
Reducing the structural weight of spacecraft can potentially save hundreds of thousands of dollars in launch costs.
Current high performance composite technology has reduced the structural weight to approximately 6-8% of the spacecraft's total dry weight.
Aluminum was the structural material of choice up to the early 1990s, accounting for approximately 18% of the spacecraft's total dry weight.
Lightweight composites such as graphite/epoxy and Kevlar/epoxy were introduced in the early 1990s to reduce structural mass while increasing strength and stiffness.
Current composite spacecraft structures require expensive secondary shielding materials to protect against electromagnetic interference and electrostatic discharge.
